subject: Historia
title: Voyages of discovery and the Renaissance
sourceSummary: The Renaissance and humanism, the breakthrough of the printing press, why European sailors sought new routes across the oceans, what the encounter between Europe and America led to, and the Reformation in brief.
topics: the encounter between Europe and America

questions.prompt: What does the word Renaissance mean?
questions.opener: The word refers to something old being given new life — namely the art and ideas of antiquity.
choices: Rebirth
Discovery
Change
Freedom
questions.explanation: Renaissance means rebirth and refers to the art, literature and science of ancient Greece and Rome once again becoming models in Europe, above all from 15th-century Italy. So the word isn't about discoveries, even though the voyages of discovery took place during the same period.

questions.prompt: What characterised humanism during the Renaissance?
questions.opener: Think about what moved to the centre of interest — alongside religion.
choices: That only priests were allowed to study
That all religion was banned
That the human being, their abilities and this world were placed at the centre of study and art
That people stopped reading ancient texts
questions.explanation: The humanists were interested in human beings themselves: their body, reason, language and possibilities in earthly life, and they eagerly studied the texts of antiquity in the original. Religion wasn't banned — most humanists were Christian — but the emphasis shifted from solely the heavenly to also the human.

questions.prompt: What was Johannes Gutenberg's great contribution around the year 1450?
questions.opener: Before him, every book was written by hand, letter by letter.
choices: He invented paper
He developed the printing press with movable metal type, so books could be printed quickly and cheaply
He built Europe's first university
He invented spectacles
questions.explanation: Gutenberg combined the printing press, printing ink and reusable cast metal letter type, which made it possible to print many identical books. Paper had been known for some time before and came from China via the Arab world, and universities already existed during the Middle Ages.

questions.prompt: What was the most important reason for the great European voyages of discovery?
questions.opener: Think about what was extremely valuable in Europe but grew far away in Asia.
choices: People wanted to draw the world's first map
People wanted to flee from the Black Death
Europe had run out of wood
People wanted to find a sea route to Asia in order to trade in spices, silk and other precious goods
questions.explanation: Spices such as pepper and cinnamon, as well as silk and porcelain, were extremely valuable in Europe, but the land routes east were long and controlled by middlemen. So the Portuguese and Spanish sought their own sea route — the pursuit of wealth, together with better ships, the compass and missionary zeal, was the driving force. Maps had been drawn for a long time already, and the Black Death had been over for more than a hundred years.

questions.prompt: What happened when Christopher Columbus sailed west in 1492?
questions.opener: He believed he had reached a completely different place from where he actually landed.
choices: He reached islands in the Caribbean but believed himself that he had arrived in India
He sailed around the entire Earth
He found the sea route around Africa to India
He reached Australia
questions.explanation: Columbus landed on islands in the Caribbean and was convinced he had reached the outskirts of Asia — which is why the inhabitants were long mistakenly called Indians. The sea route around Africa to India was sailed by Vasco da Gama in 1498, and the first circumnavigation of the world was carried out by Magellan's expedition in 1519-1522.

questions.prompt: What did Martin Luther set in motion in 1517?
questions.opener: He directed criticism at the Catholic Church, among other things at indulgences.
choices: A crusade to Jerusalem
A circumnavigation of the world
The Reformation, which led to the founding of Protestant churches
A ban on printing books
questions.explanation: Luther published his 95 Theses criticising, among other things, the sale of indulgences, and argued that faith and the Bible, not the Church's intermediaries, were what mattered. This led to the Reformation and to new Protestant churches — and Luther in fact made use of the printing press to spread his writings quickly across Europe.

questions.topic: the encounter between Europe and America
questions.prompt: Explain the important consequences of the encounter between Europe and America after 1492.
questions.opener: Split the consequences up: what happened to the people, what happened to the goods, and what happened to the power?
questions.answer: The encounter had very great consequences on both sides of the Atlantic. Diseases that the Europeans brought with them, above all smallpox and measles, hit the indigenous population of America hard since they lacked immunity, and the population fell sharply. Spain and Portugal conquered large areas and built up colonies where silver, gold and later sugar and cotton were extracted, which made European states rich and gave them greater power in the world. Labour for the plantations was obtained through the transatlantic slave trade from Africa. At the same time, new crops spread: potatoes, maize and tomatoes came to Europe and changed food here, while horses, wheat and cattle were brought to America.
steps: Diseases from Europe spread to a population without immunity, and the indigenous population of America fell sharply.
Spain and Portugal, and later other countries, turned large areas into colonies and took over power there.
Silver, gold and crops were brought to Europe and made European states richer and more powerful.
Labour for the colonies was obtained through the transatlantic slave trade from Africa.
New crops spread in both directions: potatoes, maize and tomatoes to Europe, horses, wheat and cattle to America.

questions.prompt: Summarise the Renaissance, the printing press, the voyages of discovery and the Reformation.
questions.opener: Four great changes during the same era — take them in turn.
questions.answer: The Renaissance: about 1350-1600, began in northern Italy (Florence), means rebirth and meant that antiquity became a model in art, architecture and science · artists such as Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo, more lifelike people and perspective in paintings · Humanism: the human being, reason and earthly life at the centre, study of the texts of antiquity in the original · The printing press: Gutenberg around 1450, movable metal type made books cheap and quick to spread, which increased literacy and spread new ideas · The voyages of discovery: driven by the pursuit of sea routes to Asia's spices and silk, by wealth, power and mission, made possible by caravels, the compass and better maps · Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498 around Africa, Columbus reached America in 1492 believing it was Asia, Magellan's expedition sailed around the world in 1519-1522 · Consequences: colonies, silver and new crops to Europe, disease and a huge population decline among America's indigenous peoples, the transatlantic slave trade · The Reformation: Martin Luther in 1517 with 95 theses, criticism of indulgences, the Bible in the vernacular, Protestant churches founded — in Sweden the Reformation was carried out by Gustav Vasa through the Riksdag of Västerås in 1527.
